text: Our train entered beneath the huge arch of the station in Pécs. Bay Ganyo and I went into the buffet. Knowing that we would be delayed here for a whole hour, I calmly settled down at a table and ordered breakfast and beer. All around me there was life—crowds! And a fine crowd at that. The Hungarians, you know, are not exactly to my taste, but as for the Hungarian women—I have nothing against them. Absorbed in the noise, I did not notice when Bay Ganyo had slipped out of the restaurant together with his saddlebags. Where was Bay Ganyo? His glass was empty. I looked around, searched the whole restaurant with my eyes—he was nowhere to be seen. I went outside onto the platform—“Bay Ganyo here, Bay Ganyo there”—no sign of him! Strange business! I thought he had gone to the carriage to check whether someone had not kicked his little rug away.

I went back into the restaurant again. There was still half an hour and more before the train was due to leave. I was drinking my beer and staring around. Every five minutes the porter rang the bell and, in an indifferent, lazy voice, announced the directions of the trains: “he-gesh-fe-ke-te-he-gi, kish-ke-resh, se-ge-din, uy-ve-dek.” Several English passengers were staring at his mouth, and he, apparently used to the attention his peculiar language attracted, grinned from ear to ear and, in an even louder and hoarser voice, continued: “uy-ve-dek, kish-ke-resh, he-gesh-fe-ke-te-he-gi”... — with emphatic stress on every syllable.

There were still about ten minutes left until the train’s departure. I settled the bill, paid for Bay Ganyo’s beer as well, and went out onto the platform with the intention of looking for him. At that time, a train was slowly entering under the station’s arch, and, imagine, in one of the carriages of this train, hanging halfway out of the window, Bay Ganyo appeared. I could not hear him because of the hissing of the locomotive. I understood what was going on. When the train stopped, he jumped to the ground, ran up to me, and told me, with a large admixture of energetic curses which, with your permission, I shall not repeat, the following:
– Let it be, brother, I’m worn out from running...
– What running, Bay Ganyo?
– What kind of running is that! Weren’t you staring off over there in the tavern...
– So? – I reply.

– Well? At that time, you know, the fellow by the door rang the bell, then I heard the machine whistle, I go out — I couldn’t let you know — I look, our train is pulling away. Good heavens! My little rug! So I took off after it, running and sprinting — never mind! At last, after a while, I saw it slow down, and I — hop! — in I got. One man shouted something startled at me — heke-meke — but I, you know, don’t take nonsense from anyone, so I glared back at him, showed him the little rug, and, well, he turned out to be an understanding man. He even laughed a little. Who could have known we’d be going back again. Hungarian business!

I, a sinful man, laughed heartily at Bay Ganyo’s adventure. Poor fellow! The train had maneuvered to enter another line, and Bay Ganyo ran, the poor thing, a full three kilometers to chase after it—after all, his little rug was inside!...
– Well, you, in your haste, forgot to pay for your beer, Bay Ganyo.
– Big deal! Don’t they fleece us enough? – replied Bay Ganyo in a tone brooking no objection.
– I paid for it.
– You had a lot of money—you paid for it. Now get in, get in quickly so we don’t have to run after the train again — said Bay Ganyo in a patronizing tone.

We entered the carriage. Bay Ganyo squatted over his saddlebags with his back to me, took out half a loaf of yellow cheese, cut himself a delicate little piece, cut off an enormous slice of bread too, and began to munch with wonderful appetite, puffing out first one cheek, then the other with each mouthful, and every now and then stretching his neck so that he could swallow the dry bread. Bay Ganyo had eaten his fill, belched once or twice, shook the crumbs into his palm, swallowed those too, muttered under his breath: “Ah, if only someone would treat me to a little wine now,” sat down opposite me, smiled good-naturedly, and after looking at me affectionately for a whole minute, said:
– Your Grace, have you traveled, have you wandered around much of the world?
– I’ve been around, Bay Ganyo, quite a bit.

– Oh, well, what a world I’ve knocked down! C... c... c... You leave Edirne, Constantinople aside, but in Wallachia! Do you believe it? That Giurgiu, Turnu Măgurele, Ploiești, Pitești, Brăila, Bucharest, Galați – wait, so I don’t lie to you, I don’t remember whether I was in Galați or not – I’ve been through them all.

Our journey to Vienna passed monotonously. I offered Bay Ganyo one of my little books so he could shorten the time by reading, but he politely declined my offer, because he had read quite a lot in his time, and considered it more practical to take a nap. Why should he stay awake for nothing; after all, he had paid money for the railway, so at least he might as well get some sleep. And he fell asleep. He fell asleep and snored so loudly that you would not need to hear the roar of the Atlas lion.

We arrived in Vienna and stopped at the traditional hotel “London.” The servants took my bag from the carriage, and asked to take Uncle Ganyo’s saddlebags too, but he, out of delicacy or who knows why, did not give them to them:

– How will you give them to him, brother, it’s rose oil – no joke, a strong smell, – he’ll reach in and take out some bottle – then go chase him! I know them. Don’t look at them as if they’re so   p o l i t e   (Bay Ganyo wanted to say   c o u r t e o u s,   but that word is still new in our lexicon, he forgot), don’t look at them as they wrap themselves around you. Why do they wrap themselves around you? Do they mean you well? Eins, zwei! Guten Morgen, and they keep trying to grab something. If not – a tip! Why do I keep watch at the hotel exit to slip out quietly... Beggars! A kreuzer for this one, a kreuzer for that one – there’s no getting out!
Since the rose oil that Bay Ganyo was carrying was indeed a rather valuable item, I recommended that he hand it over to the safe for safekeeping.

– At the cashier’s desk? – he cried out in a tone that sounded like pity for my naivety. – You scholars are strange, aren’t you? Why, how do you know what those at the cashier’s desk are like? You take your rose, wrap the end of it somewhere... Well, then? What do you do? Come now! Do you see this belt? – And Bay Ganyo lifted his wide waistcoat. – I’ll stuff all the little flasks inside it. True, it’s a bit heavy, but safe.
And Bay Ganyo turned his back to me (“there are all kinds of people in the world, who knows what this brat is too”) and began to stuff the musks behind his sash. I invited him to have lunch.
– Where shall we have lunch?
– Downstairs, in the restaurant.
– Thank you, I don’t feel like eating! Your Grace, go ahead and have your meal. I’ll wait for you here.
I am sure that as soon as I left the room, Bay Ganyo opened the lids. The man has his breakfast; why should he spend his money on a hot meal — he won’t die of hunger!

I took Bay Ganyo to the office of a Bulgarian merchant and left him there, and I myself got on the tram and went to Schönbrunn. I climbed up to the arch, looked out over Vienna and its surroundings, wandered through the alleys and the zoo, and spent a whole hour staring at the monkeys; then in the evening I returned to the hotel. Bay Ganyo was in the room. He wanted to conceal what he was doing, but he failed, and I noticed that he was sewing a new pocket onto the inside of his anteriya. He, being an experienced man, wore even in summer a little anteriya under his French clothes: “In winter it brings bread, in summer it brings clothes,” say the old people; that is how Bay Ganyo does too.
– I sat down to patch myself up a little, he said sheepishly.
“Are you sewing on some kind of pocket? You must have hit something from the rose oil,” I joked.

– Who, me? You’re mistaken! Why would I need a pocket here? Pockets, there are ma-a-any, as long as there’s money. No pocket, no nothing; well, my clothes had gotten a little torn, so I put on a little rag... Where were you? Out for a walk? You did well.
– Didn’t you go for a walk, Bay Ganyo, to see Vienna?

– What am I supposed to look at in Vienna? A city like any other: people, houses, finery. And wherever you go, it’s always “guten Morgen,” always they want money. Why should we give our money to the Germans — we have people here who can eat it too...
